title: Prompt caching
point: Put byte-stable content first so repeated calls reuse a cached prefix at about a tenth of the input price, and check cache-read counts to prove it works.
definition: Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processed form of a prompt prefix that exactly matches an earlier one. Matching content is billed at a reduced cache-read rate, while the first write costs slightly more than normal input.

objective.text: Given a prompt layout, reorder it so stable content sits before the cache breakpoint, remove silent invalidators, and compute the prefix cost with and without caching.

misconceptions.claim: Caching works on any repeated content, wherever it appears in the prompt.
misconceptions.correction: The cache matches a prefix byte for byte from the start. One changed byte early in the prompt invalidates everything after it, so stable content must come first.

misconceptions.claim: Once caching is switched on, the saving is guaranteed.
misconceptions.correction: A timestamp in the system prompt, unsorted JSON or a reordered tool list silently breaks the match. Every call then pays the higher write price, so verify with cache-read token counts.

l1: The cache matches a prefix, so order matters. Put byte-stable content first: the system prompt, tool definitions and rubric. Put variable content, such as retrieved documents and the user's message, after the cache breakpoint.
Cache reads cost about a tenth of normal input. Cache writes cost a little more than normal input, so a prefix that is written but never read again costs extra.
Caches expire after a few minutes of inactivity unless a call refreshes them. Low-traffic routes may rarely see a warm cache.
l2: An agent resends a 10,000-token prefix of system prompt, tools and rubric on each of 6 calls. At an illustrative $2 per million input tokens, that is 60,000 tokens or $0.12 per task.
With caching, the first call writes the prefix at 1.25 times the input price, or 12,500 token-equivalents. The other 5 calls read it at a tenth, or 5,000 token-equivalents.
That is 17,500 token-equivalents, or $0.035 per task instead of $0.12. Caching removes about 71 per cent of the prefix spend with no change to the answers.
l3: Now someone adds the current time to the system prompt. Every call has a new prefix, so every call misses and writes. Six writes cost 75,000 token-equivalents, or $0.15, more than no caching at all.
Other silent invalidators include request IDs in the prefix, JSON serialised with unsorted keys, and tool lists built in a different order on each call. None of them raises an error.
So verify rather than assume. Log cache-read and cache-write token counts on every call, and alert when the cache-read share of prefix tokens falls well below its usual level.
